title: Authentication & Authorization
description: Identity verification, access control, sessions, protected routes, and frontend security.

questions.title: 67. How does React authentication work?
questions.summary:
◦ Authentication verifies WHO the user is.
◦ R^ manages auth UI; backend verifies credentials and maintains trusted sessions.
questions.answer:
◦ Authentication = verifying user identity.
◦ User submits credentials through a login form.
◦ Frontend sends credentials to an authentication API over HTTPS.
◦ Backend validates credentials and establishes a session or issues tokens.
◦ R^ stores non-sensitive auth state and updates the UI.
◦ Subsequent requests include the required authentication credentials.
◦ Backend validates authentication on protected requests.
◦ Logout invalidates the session or tokens and clears frontend auth state.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Login → API request → Backend validation.
◦ Server may set an HttpOnly session cookie.
◦ Browser sends eligible cookies automatically on subsequent requests.
◦ R^ loads current user information to initialize auth state.
◦ AuthProvider or global store exposes authentication status.
◦ Protected routes display content only after the auth check.
◦ Backend remains responsible for enforcing access.
pitfalls: ◦ R^ does not provide authentication automatically.
◦ Frontend auth checks are not security boundaries.
◦ Never trust client-side role checks alone.
◦ Avoid storing sensitive credentials in localStorage.
◦ Handle loading, authenticated, and unauthenticated states.
followUps: ◦ How do you persist login after refresh?
◦ How do you handle expired sessions?
questions.recall:
◦ Login → API → Verify → Session → Auth State → Protected UI.
◦ Backend = Security Authority.

questions.title: 68. Authentication vs Authorization?
questions.summary:
◦ Authentication = WHO are you?
◦ Authorization = WHAT can you access?
questions.answer:
◦ Authentication confirms user identity.
◦ Authorization determines permitted actions and resources.
◦ Authentication typically occurs before authorization.
◦ RBAC grants permissions based on roles.
◦ Permission-based checks allow more granular control.
◦ Backend must enforce authorization for every protected operation.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Backend identifies the user through a valid session or token.
◦ Authorization middleware evaluates permissions for the requested resource.
◦ Successful checks allow the operation.
◦ Failed checks reject access.
◦ R^ may hide unauthorized UI elements for usability, not security.
pitfalls: ◦ Hidden buttons do not prevent unauthorized API calls.
◦ Authentication does not imply permission.
◦ Never trust client-provided roles without server validation.
questions.recall:
◦ AuthN → Identity.
◦ AuthZ → Permissions.
◦ Backend → Enforce both.

questions.title: 69. How do protected routes work?
questions.summary:
◦ Route guards check auth state before rendering protected UI.
◦ Unauthorized users are redirected or shown an access-denied page.
questions.answer:
◦ Protected routes restrict which UI authenticated users can access.
◦ A guard checks loading, authenticated, and unauthenticated states.
◦ Loading → Display fallback while verifying session.
◦ Authenticated → Render protected content.
◦ Unauthenticated → Redirect to login.
◦ Preserve intended destination to redirect after successful login.
◦ Backend independently protects the underlying data and APIs.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Router matches the requested route.
◦ Guard reads auth state from Context or store.
◦ Guard decides whether to render Outlet or Navigate.
◦ Auth state changes trigger re-r().
◦ Router updates the displayed route.
pitfalls: ◦ Avoid redirecting before session initialization finishes.
◦ Client-side route guards do not secure APIs.
◦ Prevent redirect loops.
◦ Preserve intended destination when appropriate.
followUps: ◦ How do you redirect back after login?
◦ How do you prevent unauthorized content flashing?
questions.recall:
◦ Route → Auth Check → Loading / Allow / Redirect.
◦ Guard = UI Control, not Backend Security.

questions.title: 70. JWT vs Session-based authentication?
questions.summary:
◦ JWT = signed token containing claims.
◦ Session = server-managed authentication state referenced by an identifier.
questions.answer:
◦ JWT is a token format containing claims and a cryptographic signature.
◦ A signed JWT can be verified without a database lookup, depending on architecture.
◦ Session-based auth commonly stores session state on the server.
◦ Browser sends a session identifier, usually through a cookie.
◦ Both approaches can use cookies.
◦ JWT is not automatically more secure than sessions.
◦ Choose based on architecture, revocation requirements, and security needs.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ JWT typically contains header, payload, and signature.
◦ Backend validates signature, expiration, issuer, and audience where applicable.
◦ Session auth resolves an identifier to server-side session data.
◦ Expiration and revocation policies determine session validity.
pitfalls: ◦ JWT payload is encoded, not encrypted by default.
◦ Never trust a decoded JWT without verification.
◦ JWT revocation requires additional design.
◦ Cookies can transport either session IDs or tokens.
questions.recall:
◦ JWT → Signed Claims.
◦ Session → Server State + Session ID.
◦ Both → Backend Validation.

questions.title: 71. Where should authentication tokens be stored?
questions.summary:
◦ Prefer secure, HttpOnly cookies for browser sessions when appropriate.
◦ Storage choice affects XSS and CSRF risks.
questions.answer:
◦ Browser authentication commonly uses secure, HttpOnly cookies.
◦ HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from directly reading the cookie.
◦ Secure restricts cookie transmission to HTTPS.
◦ SameSite controls certain cross-site cookie behavior.
◦ localStorage is accessible to JavaScript and exposed if malicious scripts execute.
◦ Cookie-based authentication requires appropriate CSRF protections.
◦ Storage decisions depend on the application's threat model.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Server sends Set-Cookie with appropriate attributes.
◦ Browser stores the cookie and sends it when request rules permit.
◦ R^ does not need direct access to an HttpOnly cookie.
◦ Frontend can request /api/me to determine authenticated state.
pitfalls: ◦ HttpOnly does not eliminate XSS risks.
◦ SameSite alone may not satisfy every CSRF requirement.
◦ Never store passwords in browser storage.
◦ Cross-origin cookie requests require compatible CORS and cookie settings.
questions.recall:
◦ HttpOnly → No JS Cookie Access.
◦ Secure → HTTPS.
◦ SameSite → Cross-site Rules.
◦ Backend → Session Validation.

questions.title: 72. How do access and refresh tokens work?
questions.summary:
◦ Access token authorizes API requests.
◦ Refresh token obtains a new access token after expiration.
questions.answer:
◦ Access token = short-lived credential for protected API requests.
◦ Refresh token = longer-lived credential used to request new access tokens.
◦ Expired access token may cause HTTP 401.
◦ Client can request a refreshed token through a dedicated endpoint.
◦ Successful refresh allows the original request to be retried.
◦ Failed refresh should clear auth state and require login.
◦ Refresh token rotation can reduce replay risks.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ API validates access token before processing a protected request.
◦ On expiration, refresh endpoint validates refresh credentials.
◦ Backend issues a new access token and may rotate refresh token.
◦ API client retries the failed request after successful refresh.
◦ Concurrent 401 responses should avoid triggering redundant refresh operations.
pitfalls: ◦ Avoid infinite refresh/retry loops.
◦ Do not refresh on every failed HTTP response.
◦ Refresh failure must terminate the authenticated session.
◦ Protect refresh credentials from exposure.
followUps: ◦ How do you handle simultaneous 401 responses?
◦ How does RTK Query baseQueryWithReauth work?
questions.recall:
◦ Access → API.
◦ Expired → 401 → Refresh → Retry.
◦ Refresh Fails → Logout.

questions.title: 73. How do you persist authentication after refresh?
questions.summary:
◦ R^ state resets after browser refresh.
◦ Restore auth state by validating an existing session with the backend.
questions.answer:
◦ R^ state exists in memory and resets after a full page reload.
◦ Browser may retain a valid authentication cookie.
◦ On app initialization, request current user information.
◦ Backend validates the session and returns user data.
◦ Update auth state based on the response.
◦ Keep an initialization/loading state until verification finishes.
◦ Redirect to login only after determining the user is unauthenticated.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Browser loads application.
◦ AuthBootstrap requests /api/me.
◦ Browser includes eligible session cookies.
◦ Backend validates the session.
◦ Auth store updates user + status.
◦ Protected routes render according to verified auth state.
pitfalls: ◦ Do not treat persisted frontend flags as proof of authentication.
◦ Avoid unauthorized UI flashes.
◦ Distinguish network failures from invalid sessions.
◦ Handle session expiration after initialization.
followUps: ◦ Why does auth state disappear after refresh?
◦ How do you prevent redirect flicker?
questions.recall: ◦ Reload → AuthBootstrap → /me → Verify → Restore State → Render.

questions.title: 74. How do you handle authentication errors?
questions.summary:
◦ 401 → Missing or invalid authentication.
◦ 403 → Authenticated but insufficient permission, or access otherwise forbidden.
questions.answer:
◦ HTTP 401 indicates valid authentication credentials are missing or not accepted.
◦ HTTP 403 indicates the server refuses access, commonly due to insufficient permissions.
◦ Handle 401 by checking whether session refresh is supported.
◦ Retry after successful refresh where appropriate.
◦ If authentication cannot be restored, require login.
◦ Handle 403 with an access-denied UI.
◦ Display safe, understandable errors to users.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ API returns an HTTP error response.
◦ API client classifies response status.
◦ Authentication layer may attempt one refresh for eligible 401 responses.
◦ Authorization errors are handled separately.
◦ R^ updates error or auth state, triggering re-r().
pitfalls: ◦ Do not automatically retry every 401 indefinitely.
◦ Do not treat 403 as a refresh-token problem by default.
◦ Avoid exposing sensitive backend error details.
◦ Network errors are not necessarily authentication failures.
followUps: ◦ How do you handle network failures?
◦ How do you avoid retry loops?
questions.recall:
◦ 401 → Authenticate / Refresh.
◦ 403 → Forbidden / Permission.
◦ Network Error ≠ Invalid Session.

questions.title: 75. How do you implement secure logout?
questions.summary:
◦ Logout invalidates authentication on the backend.
◦ Frontend clears auth state and protected cached data.
questions.answer:
◦ Logout should invalidate the server-side session or revoke relevant credentials when supported.
◦ Backend clears or expires authentication cookies.
◦ R^ clears authenticated user state.
◦ Clear sensitive cached API data and user-specific state.
◦ Redirect to login or public content.
◦ Protect against displaying another user's cached data after account changes.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Frontend sends logout request.
◦ Backend invalidates session or refresh credentials.
◦ Backend expires authentication cookie when applicable.
◦ Frontend resets auth state and private caches.
◦ Protected routes react to the unauthenticated state.
pitfalls: ◦ Clearing R^ state alone does not invalidate a server session.
◦ HttpOnly cookies cannot be deleted directly through JavaScript.
◦ Clear user-specific cached data.
◦ Handle logout request failures according to the application's security policy.
followUps: ◦ How do you invalidate a session?
◦ What should happen to Redux/RTK Query cache?
◦ How do you handle logout across multiple tabs?
questions.recall: ◦ Logout → Backend Invalidate → Clear Cookie → Reset State/Cache → Redirect.
